prompt: Some say that music, art and drama are as important as other school subjects, especially at the primary level. Do you agree or disagree?
intro_note: Band-7 rewrite of the original W5 essay keeping the writer's own two reasons and examples (K-pop training, drawing/melodies). It applies the examiner panel's agreed fixes: creative-subjects register, explicit subjects in long sentences, bare plurals for generic nouns, a completed PEEL link, and a synthesising conclusion. Hover any highlight for the craft note and what it fixes.

spans.text: It is sometimes claimed that
creative subjects such as music, art and drama

highlight.label: Names the category correctly
highlight.explanation: The original called them "minor subjects" four times — quietly arguing against its own thesis that they are equal. "Creative subjects" / "arts subjects" is the neutral exam-register label, and the essay rotates these labels instead of repeating one.

spans.text: deserve the same status as core subjects, particularly at primary school.
I fully agree with this view

highlight.label: Agreement + register fix
highlight.explanation: Fixes the original thesis sentence "This essay totally agree with that statement": the verb needed -s, and "totally" is spoken register. An error in the sentence an examiner reads first is the most expensive kind.

spans.text: , because
early exposure to the arts

highlight.label: Natural collocation
highlight.explanation: Replaces "in the early stage" — the natural collocations are "at an early age" / "early exposure to X". Collocation precision is the panel's #1 focus area for this writer.

spans.text: helps children discover their hidden talents and
trains the kind of open-ended thinking that single-answer subjects rarely exercise

highlight.label: Roadmap with content
highlight.explanation: The introduction previews BOTH body reasons in fresh words (talent discovery + creative thinking). The bodies then deliver exactly these two — the no-drift discipline W4's Body 2 slipped on.

spans.text: Schools should value

highlight.label: Generic plural — no "the"
highlight.explanation: The original wrote "the school should treat". Generic reference takes a bare plural (schools, students, pupils) — this writer's most persistent error class, seen in W3, W4 and W5. Every generic noun in this model uses the bare plural.

spans.text: arts subjects
just as highly as academic ones

highlight.label: Equative comparison
highlight.explanation: The pattern is "just as X as Y" (or "equally X" with no "as"). The original conclusion fused the two into "equally important as".

spans.text: chiefly because every child has a unique talent, and
the earlier it is spotted, the more room it has to grow

highlight.label: The more…, the more…
highlight.explanation: A comparative correlative — short, safe Band-7 range that appears nowhere in W1–W5. One of the panel's stretch goals: structures to attempt, not just errors to avoid.

spans.text: . Once students reach secondary school,
entrance exams begin to dominate their timetables

highlight.label: Collocation upgrade
highlight.explanation: Replaces "spend more time on preparing university's entrance exam" (preposition + possessive errors, flat phrasing). "Exams dominate timetables" is precise, active and article-safe.

spans.text: so they lose the chance to explore these disciplines and may never fully develop their abilities

highlight.label: Subject survives the sentence
highlight.explanation: The original collapsed here: "…and eventually, cannot develop their talents" — the subject vanished before "cannot" (Korean topic-drop). Every coordinated verb keeps its subject: THEY lose … and MAY never develop. "These disciplines" also continues the label rotation.

spans.text: . For example,
since many K-pop artists begin systematic training in their early teens

highlight.label: Plural fixed, example kept
highlight.explanation: Keeps the writer's own K-pop example but fixes "when they are teenager" (missing plural) and upgrades "a lot of" (spoken register) to "many".

spans.text: a child whose musical talent is noticed in a primary school music class stands a far better chance of being ready in time

highlight.label: PEEL link completed
highlight.explanation: The original example proved early training matters but never mentioned school. This clause supplies the missing link — the talent is spotted IN a school music class — using a defining relative clause ("whose…") for grammatical range.

spans.text: Primary school is therefore the only stage at which every child, not just a lucky few, gets that opportunity.

highlight.label: Paragraph link-back
highlight.explanation: A closing sentence ties the example back to the claim — the L of PEEL, missing from every W1–W4 body paragraph. "The only stage at which…" adds a preposition + relative structure.

spans.text: A further reason for taking the arts seriously

highlight.label: 8-word topic sentence
highlight.explanation: Replaces the original's 30–40-word frame ("The second main reason why teaching those minor subjects is important especially for elementary school students is that…"). Short claim first, support after — and "the arts" continues the label rotation.

spans.text: is that they teach children to think in more inventive ways.
Most academic subjects, such as mathematics or science, lead to a single correct answer, whereas creative subjects do not

highlight.label: Kept from your original
highlight.explanation: Your "whereas" contrast was already error-free Band-7 grammar — the panel's What's-working note. The model keeps your best sentence almost unchanged (only "the subjects like music, art and drama" → bare "creative subjects").

spans.text: a portrait can be drawn in countless styles, and a melody can be composed in millions of ways

highlight.label: Example developed + passives
highlight.explanation: Develops the thin "it is possible to draw a person in various ways, and there are millions of unique mdelodies" into a balanced pair, adds two passives for range, and fixes the "melodies" spelling.

spans.text: . Pupils therefore learn that some problems have many good solutions, and
this habit of mind

highlight.label: Summary-noun reference
highlight.explanation: "This + summary noun" refers back to the whole previous idea without repeating it — the reference-and-substitution device Band 7 CC asks for, replacing repeated noun phrases.

spans.text: later enriches even their academic work.
In conclusion,
because talent surfaces early and creativity cannot be learned from an answer key

highlight.label: Synthesis, not restatement
highlight.explanation: The original conclusion repeated the introduction almost verbatim — the recurring W2/W4 problem. This compresses both body arguments into fresh imagery ("an answer key") instead.

spans.text: , I believe
primary schools should give music, art and drama just as much weight as any core subject

highlight.label: Bare plural + fixed equative
highlight.explanation: "Primary schools" (generic bare plural, not "the school") and "just as much weight as" (not "equally important as") — the writer's two recurring grammar classes, both correct in the sentence that leaves the final impression.
